summary: This Level 3 unit teaches you to plan and lead the manual handling of electrical materials and equipment: cable drums, panels, batteries, long lengths, and heavy items fixed at height. You will assess the load, the route and the people, choose handling aids, use safe lifting and team-lifting methods, lead a team cable pull, check lifting gear, prevent long-term strain injuries and report incidents.

blocks.p: Electrical work moves heavy things: cable drums, distribution boards, battery banks, transformers, cable tray and air-conditioning units. Most of it is moved by people. Back and shoulder injuries are among the most common in the trade, and many build up slowly over years. At Level 3 you do more than lift safely yourself: you **plan the move, choose the method and the aids, lead the team and see that nobody is hurt**.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Plan the move
Find the load's weight, size and centre of gravity, walk the route, and write a lift plan for heavy or awkward items.
Avoid handling where you can
Use goods lifts, hoists, deliveries to the point of use and assembly at ground level before you decide to carry.
Lift and carry safely
Use a sound technique, keep loads close, and know when a load is too heavy for one person.
Lead team lifts
Name one leader, agree the moves and signals, and make sure every move is made together.
Handle cable drums
Unload, roll, chock, mount and pay out drums safely.
Lead a team cable pull
Set up the drum, name the leader, agree signals and stop the pull when it sticks.
Handle batteries and long items
Control acid, short circuits and hydrogen; carry long ladders and conduit clear of people and overhead lines.
Choose and check handling aids and lifting gear
Check ratings, tags and condition, and tag out any faulty aid.
Move and fix heavy items at height
Use lift aids and platforms, support the load while it is fixed, and control the area below.
Prevent strain injuries and report incidents
Spot early signs, organise work to cut the risk, and report accidents and near misses.

ul: Jamaica's **heat and humidity** tire people sooner, and sweaty hands lose their grip. Plan breaks, water and shade for long handling jobs.
**Rain** makes drums, steps and ramps slippery, and **wind** catches solar panels, ladders and sheets of tray like sails.
Many sites have **steep or uneven ground**, narrow staircases and no goods lift. Plan the route before the truck arrives.
Overhead JPS lines run beside many yards and roofs. A long metal ladder or length of conduit that touches one can kill the person holding it.
Employers have a duty to protect workers from injury at work, and workers must use the controls provided and report hazards. The Centre's and the employer's own safety rules set this out.

blocks.note: No lift is so urgent that it cannot be planned. The few minutes you spend assessing the load and route cost far less than a day's pay lost to a strained back, or a lifetime of pain. If a load is too heavy, awkward or unsafe, say so and ask for an aid or more people.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: The sections follow a job: understanding the harm, assessing the risk, lifting, using aids, then the special loads of the trade, and finally planning and leading. Work the sums with a calculator. Weights, loads and distances in this kit are typical: for real equipment use the maker's data, the marked rating on each aid and your instructor's rules.

Manual handling means moving or supporting a load by hand or by bodily force: lifting, lowering, pushing, pulling, carrying and holding. Injuries from it are called **musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs)**: damage to muscles, tendons, ligaments, joints and the spine.

head: Injury
What happens
How it comes about
rows: Strain or sprain
A muscle is overstretched or torn (strain); a ligament at a joint is overstretched or torn (sprain)
A sudden heavy lift, a twist under load, a slip while carrying
Back injury
Damage to muscles, ligaments or the discs between the bones of the spine; pain, stiffness, sometimes nerve pain in the legs
Bending and twisting while lifting, repeated heavy lifting, lifting from low down, awkward loads
Hernia
A weakness in the wall of the abdomen lets part of the gut push through
Lifting something very heavy, especially with a held breath
Shoulder and neck injury
Pain and weakness from loading the shoulder
Overhead work, carrying on the shoulder, reaching with a load
Hand and wrist injury
Cuts, crush injuries, tendon strain
Sharp edges on tray and trunking, trapped fingers, gripping hard for long
Foot and toe injury
Crushing
A dropped drum, panel or box

ul: **Sudden injuries**: a single lift or slip, the sharp pain you feel at once.

**Gradual injuries**: wear that builds up over months and years from awkward postures, repeated movements and moderately heavy loads, with no single bad moment. Most back and shoulder trouble in electricians is like this.

Early signs of gradual injury are **aches or stiffness that keep coming back**, particularly after work or in the morning. They are the body's warning. A team leader treats them seriously and looks again at the job.

blocks.h: The spine and why technique matters

blocks.p: The spine is a stack of small bones with discs between them. When you bend forward from the waist to lift, the discs are squeezed unevenly and the muscles of the lower back carry a very large force, far more than the weight of the load. Bending the knees and keeping the back straight lets the **big leg muscles do the work** and keeps the load on the discs even. This is why 'bend your knees, not your back' is the first rule.

blocks.note: The back gets **more** vulnerable when it is twisted, when the load is held away from the body, when the lift is from the floor or above the shoulders, and when you are tired or hot. Change the job so these things do not happen together.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Who
Must
rows: Employer or Centre
Assess the risk, provide aids and training, avoid hazardous handling where it can be avoided, and act on reports
Supervisor or team leader
Plan the move, brief the team, name a leader for team lifts, check the aids and watch for strain
Every worker
Use the aids and methods provided, follow the plan, not attempt a load that needs more help, and **report** pain, near misses and faulty equipment

sections.title: Assessing the risk: load, task, environment, person

blocks.p: Before moving anything heavy, awkward or repeated, ask four questions. Put together they are often called **TILE**: Task, Individual, Load, Environment.

head: Heading
Ask
Examples in electrical work
rows: Task
Does it involve twisting, stooping, reaching above the shoulders, long carries, pushing or pulling, a rush, or no rest?
Drilling overhead for hours; carrying tray up three flights; pulling cable with no breaks
Individual
Does it need unusual strength? Is the person new, young, tired, hurt, pregnant, or not trained? Is PPE or clothing restricting?
A trainee on the first week; someone with a bad back; someone in a tight harness
Load
Is it heavy, bulky, hard to grip, unstable, hot, sharp or awkward? Does it shift or have its weight at one end?
A 180 kg distribution panel; a long ladder; a top-heavy control panel; a lead-acid battery
Environment
Are there steps, slopes, wet or uneven floors, narrow doors, poor light, heat, wind, or overhead lines?
A flooded yard; a roof in gusty wind; a plant room reached only by a narrow stair

blocks.h: Weights you must be able to work out

ul: **Mass of cable** = mass per metre × length. A 100 m coil at 0.35 kg/m has 35 kg of cable. Add the reel or drum: with a 6 kg reel, the total is 41 kg.
**Several identical items**: 6 batteries of 28 kg = 168 kg.
**Bundles**: 12 lengths of 3 m conduit at 0.9 kg per metre = 12 × 3 × 0.9 = 32.4 kg.
**Aid ratings**: a trolley rated for 150 kg carries boxes of 18 kg each: 150 ÷ 18 = 8.3, so at most **8** boxes (round down). With 100 kg already on it, the rest is 50 kg, or two 18 kg boxes.
Allow for the **drum or packaging** and for any tools on the load.

blocks.p: There is no single 'safe' weight: it depends on the person, the posture, how close the load is held and how often it is lifted. A common guide is that a load a fit adult can lift from the floor close to the body, once, is limited to about 25 kg for men and 16 kg for women, and much less held away from the body, high up, or repeated. For a team the common guide is that two people lift **about two-thirds** of the sum of what each could lift alone, three people about **half**, because they cannot share the load perfectly. Treat such figures as warnings, not permission: assess every lift and use an aid whenever the load is heavy, awkward or the job is repeated.

blocks.note: **Example.** Three trainees who could each lift 25 kg alone try to share a 60 kg panel. Sum of capacities: 75 kg. Three people manage about half: 37.5 kg. The 60 kg panel is **too heavy for them to carry safely**, so a trolley, a lift aid or more people is needed.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Level
Handling example
rows: 1. Avoid handling
Have the supplier deliver to the point of use; use the goods lift or a hoist; assemble hangers and splice tray on the ground, not at height
2. Use a mechanical aid
Trolley, sack truck, pallet truck, drum stand, chain block, platform lift, vacuum lifter
3. Reduce the load
Smaller packs; split bundles; move fewer boxes at a time
4. Improve the task and the place
Store heavy items at waist height; clear the route; light the stairs; platform at the right height for overhead work
5. Train and supervise
Safe technique, team lifting, signals; check understanding

blocks.p: Start at the top. Training and technique are the last resort, because people get tired and make mistakes.

blocks.h: A safe lift, step by step

flow: Stop and think: weight, route, where it goes, who helps
Check the load for sharp edges, grease, a heavy end, loose parts
Feet apart, one slightly forward, balanced and stable
Bend the knees; keep the back straight; head up
Get a firm grip, palms and fingers, not fingertips
Hold the load **close to the body**, between waist and chest height
Lift smoothly with the legs; no jerking and no twisting
Move your feet to turn; never twist the back with a load
Look where you are going; set the load down the same way, bending the knees

head: Do
Do not
rows: Keep the load close, at waist height
Hold it out in front with straight arms
Turn by moving the feet
Twist the body while holding the load
Keep the **heavy end** of a marked box nearest your body
Drag it by the light end
Split a load that is too heavy
Carry on a shoulder, or on your head, up stairs
Use both hands and good grip gloves where edges are sharp
Lift with wet, greasy or sweaty hands
Rest and sip water in the heat
Keep lifting when tired: fatigue causes most slips

ul: Plan the route, clear it, check the doors are open and the floor is dry.
Keep your view clear. If you cannot see over the load, it needs a spotter or a different method.
Stairs: split the load, or use two people or a hoist. Never carry a heavy load on stairs alone.
Put the load down at rest points, and set it down gently, bending your knees.
Do not carry loads **up a ladder**: you need both hands to climb. Use a rope, a hoist or a platform.
**Push** rather than pull where you can: pushing uses body weight and keeps you looking forward.
Keep the back straight, push with your legs, with hands between waist and shoulder height.
A load on wheels is much easier than a dragged one, but a heavy load on a slope can run away. On a ramp, control it with a rope, and nobody stands below.
Check that casters and tyres work and that the floor is smooth and clear.

blocks.p: Wear **safety boots and gloves with a good grip** for metal trunking, cable tray, drums and boxes of fittings. Cut-resistant gloves matter for sheet steel edges; a good grip stops slips. Gloves do not make the load lighter, and they do not replace the aid you should have used.

ul: A team lift needs **one named leader** who calls the move: 'Ready? Lift!' Everyone lifts together, on the command, not when each person is ready.
Team members should be about the same height and strength, so the load is level and shared.
Agree beforehand where the load is going, who walks backwards (nobody should: have a spotter), where the rests are and how to set it down: 'Lower!'
A **spotter** (banksman) walks beside or ahead to watch the route, clear people and warn of hazards.
No talking over each other: one voice only. Anyone can call 'Stop!'
Where two people carry a long load, carry it on the same shoulder, or at the same height at each end, with the front end a little high so the carrier can see ahead.

blocks.note: Two trainees carrying a long panel, both talking, with nobody leading, is an accident waiting to happen. Stop them, name a leader, and agree the moves before they pick it up again.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Aid
Best for
Cautions
rows: Sack truck (hand truck)
Boxes, small drums, batteries, over level ground
Strap the load; do not overload; take stairs one step at a time with two people
Flat trolley
Several boxes; a panel strapped upright; long corridors
Rated load; strap tall loads so they cannot tip; push, do not pull
Pallet truck
Pallets of conduit, cable or fittings
Smooth, level floors only: not slopes, stairs or soft ground
Dolly or machine skates
Heavy panels and transformers over short distances on a floor
Keep the load centred; use enough skates; push slowly
Drum stand or jacks
Paying out cable; lifting a drum off the ground
Spindle through the drum; brake fitted; base level and firm
Chain block or hoist
Lifting heavy items up, such as a transformer or a motor
Check rating, tag and hook catch; fix to a point rated for the load
Gin wheel (pulley) and rope
Raising materials to a roof or scaffold
Rated gear; tag line; nobody below
Platform lift or scissor lift
Lifting heavy items to wall brackets or to ceilings
Trained operators; firm level floor
Ramp with control ropes
Unloading a drum or heavy item from a vehicle
Ramp rated for the load, strong and secured; ropes held by people to the side

head: Check
Why
rows: **Rated load** (safe working load) marked, and greater than the load
Overloaded gear breaks
**Test tag or inspection record** in date
Shows a competent person has examined it
Chain block: links not stretched or damaged; brake works; **hook has a working safety catch**, not opened out or cracked
A failed link or hook drops the load
Slings and straps: no cuts, burns, knots, frays or chemical damage
Damage cuts the strength
Trolley or truck: wheels, tyres, frame, straps
A collapse mid-move injures people
Drum stand: jacks, spindle, level and firm base
A drum falling off its stand can crush
The thing it hangs from, such as a beam or gantry: rated for the load
The gear can be fine and the support still fail

ul: **Never exceed the rated load.** Know the weight before the lift, and use gear whose rating is clearly above it.
Lifting gear for lifting people, or equipment that has never been examined, is never used.
Gear that **slips, drops its load, makes odd noises or shows damage** is stopped at once.

Faulty gear is **tagged out of use, reported, recorded and kept apart** until it is repaired or scrapped. Carrying on with 'lighter loads', oiling it and trying again, or telling nobody because 'nothing was damaged', all leave the next person to pay.

blocks.h: Slings and weights on the legs

blocks.p: When a sling lifts a load, the load in each leg depends on the angle between the legs. The wider the angle, the more load in each leg. For two legs and a vertical angle of 60° between them, each leg carries about the same as half the load when the legs are vertical, **times 1.15**; wider angles give much more, so the sling's rating falls. A sling used in a choke hitch or at a wide angle carries less than the rating marked for a straight lift. Always work from the sling's tag and the maker's table for the way it is used.

blocks.note: A chain sling whose tag shows its last thorough examination was 14 months ago, where the rule is every 6 months, is **out of date and must not be used** until it is examined again.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Cable drums and team cable pulling

blocks.p: A drum of armoured cable can weigh several hundred kilograms. It can roll, crush a foot or a person, and cause the cable to be damaged if it is handled badly.

head: Stage
Safe method
rows: Unloading from a truck
A **ramp with control ropes**, a tail lift, or a crane or forklift with a **spindle through the centre hole** and a spreader. Never drop it onto sandbags or tyres, or have people catch it.
Rolling
Only on firm, level ground, in the direction of the **arrow painted on the flange**, so that the cable layers do not loosen. Never roll it flat on a flange or spin it.
On a slope
Control it with ropes; people stay out of its path and **never stand below it**. Roll it only if there is no better way.
Standing in store or on site
On its flanges, **chocked** on both sides so it cannot roll; cable ends sealed; under cover.
Lifting by crane
Spindle through the centre hole with a spreader bar or a sling arrangement rated for the load. **Not** slings round the cable, and not by hooking one flange.
Paying out cable
Spindle through the centre hole; drum raised on **drum jacks** or a stand so it turns freely; a **brake** or a person ready to slow it so it does not over-run; cable pulled off the **top**.

ul: Wear gloves and safety boots throughout, and keep your feet clear of the flanges.
A drum off its chocks, even if it hit nobody, is a **near miss** to be reported, so the cause is fixed before someone is hurt.

flow: Check the route is clear and smooth, with a draw wire or rope in place
Work out the cable's weight and length
Set up the drum on jacks with a spindle and brake; place a feeder there
Place pullers at the far end and at draw-in points
Name **one leader** to give the commands
Agree signals or radios so anyone can call 'Stop!' at once
Pull steadily, not in jerks
If the cable sticks, stop and find the cause
Check the cable for damage at the end

head: Rule
Why
rows: One named person gives commands
Everyone pulls together; no confusion about when to start and stop
Signals or radios if the ends cannot see each other
A trapped person or a stuck cable must be stoppable at once
Gloves on; **never wrap a pulling rope round your hand**
A sudden jerk can trap and crush or pull the hand into a pulley
Steady pull
Jerks damage the cable and strain backs
If the cable becomes very hard to move: **stop**, find the snag, then carry on
Pulling harder tears sheaths and may injure people when the snag gives way
Never tie the rope to a vehicle
A vehicle can pull far harder than anyone can control
Never pull cable through a duct that holds live cables
Contact can cut insulation and cause a fault

blocks.p: Work out the weight before the pull. A 4-core armoured cable at 6 kg per metre pulled along 55 m means **330 kg** of cable to move, plus the friction of the route. That is a job for a plan, rollers and a winch with a tension limit if the maker's data says the cable cannot be hand-pulled.

sections.title: Special loads: panels, batteries, long items and loads at height

ul: Find the **weight, size and centre of gravity** from the maker's data. A control panel is often **top-heavy**: it tips easily, so steady it and move it slowly.
Move it **strapped upright** on a trolley, dolly or pallet truck. Never tip it on its side or slide it along the floor, unless the maker says it can be.
If it is too wide for a door when upright, plan to **tilt** it safely with enough people, as the maker allows. Do not force it or cut it.
Fix a heavy board to a wall with a stand or lift supporting its weight while it is fixed, not with one person holding it while another drills.
A written **lift plan** for a heavy panel shows the weight, the route, the aids, the people, their roles and the signals.

blocks.note: **Example plan for a 200 kg panel to a first-floor plant room:** weight 200 kg and centre of gravity from the data; route walked, with a 0.9 m door and the stairs; pallet truck to the foot of the stairs; goods lift or hoist to the first floor; trolley with straps to the wall; four trained people, one leader and one spotter; platform lift to hold it while two people fix it; PPE: boots and gloves.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Hazard
Control
rows: Weight (often 25 kg and more each)
Carrying handles or a battery carrier; a trolley for longer moves; two people where needed; keep upright
Acid
Safety glasses and acid-resistant gloves; check the case for cracks; have a spill kit and washing water near
Short circuits across the terminals by a tool, watch or ring
Remove metal jewellery; fit **insulating terminal covers**; keep tools away from the top of the battery
Hydrogen given off during charging
Ventilated place; no flames or sparks; follow the maker's instructions
Placing them
On a stand rated for the total weight; with the terminals covered; in a ventilated area

blocks.p: Total mass: 8 batteries of 28 kg = **224 kg**, which the stand and the floor must take.

ul: Outdoors, a long metal ladder or length of conduit can touch an overhead line. **Look up first.** Carry long items flat and low, plan the route away from lines and keep well clear of them, as the Centre and the power company require.
Wind catches long items and sheet material. Do not move them in gusty wind.

Indoors, the ends of a long item can strike people, glass, sprinkler heads and light fittings when you turn. Carry long items with **two people, one at each end**, with the front end a little high and a clear view ahead.
Stop at corners and doors. A third person walks ahead where the route is busy.
Do not carry long conduit lengths on one shoulder, walking round blind corners.

head: Job
Method
rows: Cable coils up to a 4 m roof
**Hoist** them with a rope or hoist; never carry them up a ladder, throw them, or pass them hand to hand up a ladder
Solar panels across a roof
Two people; a tag line; not in gusty wind; set loads down away from the edge and tie or weigh them down
An air-conditioning unit of about 45 kg to wall brackets 2 m up
A **lift aid or platform** with a planned team lift; the circuit stays isolated; the unit is steadied and fixed before the aid takes its weight away
Light fittings and small items to a ceiling space
Bucket or bag on a rope from a platform; load placed on joists or boards, never the ceiling board
A mobile tower to be moved
Clear people and tools off it first, look overhead, then lock the wheels when it stops

ul: Close off the area below and have people wear hard hats. Nobody stands under a load.
Raise slowly, steady with a hand or **tag line**, and put the load on brackets or a temporary support before releasing the aid.
A tag line is a light rope attached to the load, held by a person standing clear, to stop the load swinging or spinning. It is never wrapped round the hand.
Plan so that nobody carries a heavy load up a ladder, because a person on a ladder needs both hands to climb.
Keep heavy items on **low and middle shelves**, between knee and shoulder height. Light items go higher.
Never put heavy boxes on the top shelf, in a walkway, or on top of cable drums.
Leave aisles wide enough for a trolley.

sections.title: Planning, leading, strain prevention and reporting

head: Part of the plan
Content
rows: The load
Weight, size, centre of gravity, lifting points, special hazards (acid, top-heavy, sharp)
The route
Walked beforehand: doors, steps, slopes, stairs or lift, floor, rest points, overhead lines
The aids
Which trolley, hoist, platform or drum stand; the rating; checked and in date
The people
How many, who leads, who spots, who does each job; training and fitness
Signals and communication
Commands, hand signals or radio calls; who may call 'Stop!'
Controls
PPE, exclusion zone below, barriers, supports while fixing
If something goes wrong
Who is first-aider, where is the phone, how to stop the lift safely

flow: Assess the load, the route and the people
Choose the aid; check it and its rating
Brief the team: plan, roles, signals
Walk the route and clear it
Do the move with one leader calling it
Set the load down and secure it
Review: what worked, what needs to change

ul: **Stop unsafe work.** If two people are carrying a long panel with nobody leading, stop them, name a leader and agree the moves.
Check **understanding**, not just attendance: ask a trainee to talk you through how they will move the load, and watch them do it.
Give the **least experienced** person the lighter job at first, pair them with someone experienced and rotate the jobs.
A back-support belt is not a safe way to lift heavier loads: it does not strengthen the back, and it can give a false feeling of safety. Technique, aids and planning prevent injuries.

head: Problem
What a team leader can do
rows: Overhead drilling
A platform or tower at the right height so people do not reach above the head; drill stands or extension handles; rotate the job
Repeated cable pulling and stripping
Share and rotate the tasks; short breaks; sharp tools; good grips
Carrying materials
Deliver them close to the work in small packs; use trolleys and hoists
Awkward postures
Raise the work; use kneeling pads and stands; change position often
Heat and fatigue
Shade, water and rest breaks; plan heavy lifts for the cooler part of the day
Early aches
Ask people to report them early; act on reports; look at the job again

ul: A person who feels a **sharp pain in the back while lifting** stops, gets first aid, and the incident is reported. Finishing the lift, taking a painkiller and carrying on, or swapping jobs without telling anyone all let a small injury become a large one.

**Report** every injury, near miss and unsafe condition to the supervisor, and fill in the Centre's or firm's form. A drum that rolled off its chocks and hit nobody is a near miss: report it so the cause is fixed before someone is hurt.

A good report gives the date, time and place; who was involved and who saw it; what happened in order, as facts; any injury and first aid given; the equipment and load involved; and what was done to make the area safe.
Look at the **cause**, not at who to blame: was the load assessed? Was the aid available and checked? Was the leader named? Was the person trained and not tired?
Keep records. They help to find patterns, such as the same task causing aches in several people.

blocks.note: In Jamaica, call **110** for an ambulance or the fire brigade and **119** for the police. Know where the first-aid kit and the trained first-aider are before the lift begins.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can name the main handling injuries and say how they happen, including gradual injuries.
I can explain why bending the knees and keeping the back straight protects the spine.
I can assess a move using task, individual, load and environment.
I can work out the mass of cable, a bundle of conduit, a set of batteries and the number of boxes a trolley may carry.
I can say why a team of three cannot carry the sum of what each could lift alone.
I can use the hierarchy: avoid, use an aid, reduce the load, improve the task, train.
I can describe a safe lift and a safe carry, and say when to use an aid.
I can lead a team lift with one leader, agreed signals and a spotter.
I can choose a handling aid for a given load and place.
I can check a chain block, sling, trolley and drum stand before use, and tag out a faulty one.
I can unload, roll, chock, mount and pay out a cable drum safely.
I can plan and lead a team cable pull, and stop it when the cable sticks.
I can plan the move and fixing of a heavy panel, including a lift plan.
I can move lead-acid batteries safely and explain their hazards.
I can carry long items safely and keep clear of overhead lines.
I can raise loads to a roof or ceiling space without carrying them up a ladder.
I can store heavy items where they do not injure people.
I can name ways to reduce the long-term risk of back, shoulder and wrist injury.
I can say what to do after a handling injury, and report an incident or near miss with the right details.

head: What
How
rows: Mass of cable
kg per metre × metres, plus the drum or reel
Boxes on a trolley
Rated load ÷ mass of one box, rounded down
Load still allowed on an aid
Rated load − load already on it
Team lifting guide
Two people about two-thirds of the sum of their capacities; three about a half
Lifting guide for one person
Close to the body, between waist and chest; lower and less often when held away or repeated
Cable drum
Roll in the direction of the arrow; chock when it stops; lift with a spindle
Pulling rope
Never round the hand
Ladder
Never carry a heavy load up one
Emergency numbers
110 ambulance and fire; 119 police

terms: A person who guides a moving load and warns others.
The point at which a load's weight acts; if it is high, the load tips easily.
A wedge placed against a drum or wheel so it cannot roll.
A pair of stands that lift a cable drum off the ground so it turns freely.
A pulley fixed at the top of a scaffold or roof, used with a rope to raise materials.
A written plan for moving a heavy item: its weight, route, aids, people, roles and signals.
Moving or supporting a load by hand or bodily force.
Musculoskeletal disorder: damage to muscles, tendons, ligaments, joints or the spine.
An event that could have caused injury or damage but did not.
The most load a piece of lifting gear may carry, marked on it.
A two-wheeled hand trolley with a toe plate for moving boxes and small drums.
The steel bar passed through the centre hole of a cable drum so that it can turn.
An overstretched or torn ligament at a joint.
A light rope fixed to a load, held by a person clear of it, to stop it swinging.
Task, Individual, Load, Environment: the four headings for assessing a handling risk.

c1.title: Moving a switchboard in Mandeville
c1.text: Ms Rochelle Gordon, a Level 3 electrician, must move a 240 kg floor-standing switchboard from a delivery truck at the back of a clinic in Mandeville, Manchester, to a plant room on the first floor. The route is a short slope, a doorway 0.8 m wide, and a stair with a goods hoist beside it. The board is 1.9 m tall and 0.75 m wide and is top-heavy. Three trainees, each able to lift about 25 kg alone, are available. The clinic is open to patients throughout.

c2.title: A drum and a long pull at a market in Savanna-la-Mar
c2.text: Mr Winston Lee, a Level 3 electrician, leads six trainees pulling a 4-core armoured cable into a duct along the back of a market in Savanna-la-Mar, Westmoreland. The cable weighs 4.2 kg per metre and the pull is 60 m. The drum stands on a slight slope behind the market and is not chocked. The pullers are at the far end, out of sight of the drum. A trainee says he will wind the pulling rope round his hand for a better grip.

c3.title: A solar battery bank in Lucea
c3.text: Ms Natalie Smith, a Level 3 electrician, is installing a standby battery bank for a guest house in Lucea, Hanover. There are 10 lead-acid batteries of 32 kg each, to be carried 30 m over gravel and set on a steel stand. A trainee is wearing a wedding ring and a metal watch. The terminal covers are in a bag on the truck. The stand is rated for 300 kg.

c4.title: Rooftop work in Montego Bay
c4.text: Mr Orlando Brown, a Level 3 electrician, leads the fitting of an air-conditioning unit of 48 kg and 12 solar panels on the flat roof of an office in Montego Bay, St James. The roof is reached by a vertical ladder only, and the afternoon wind is gusty. A trainee offers to carry the unit up the ladder on his shoulder. The roof edge has no parapet at the front, and a JPS line runs 4 m from the back of the building.

c5.title: A strained back at a workshop in Portmore
c5.text: At an electrical workshop in Portmore, St Catherine, a trainee named Shane felt a sharp pain in his lower back while lifting a 45 kg coil of cable alone from the floor of the store. He finished the job, took a painkiller and said nothing. Two days later he told his team leader, Ms Carla Bennett. The store's heavy boxes are kept on the top shelf, there is no trolley, and two other staff have mentioned aching backs in recent weeks.

questions.q: Three trainees can each lift about 25 kg alone. About how much can they carry together, using the usual team guide?
o: About 75 kg
About 37 kg
About 50 kg
About 25 kg
questions.why: Three people can lift about half of the sum of what each could lift alone: 3 × 25 = 75 kg, and half of that is about 37 kg. People cannot share a load perfectly, so a team lifts less than the sum. The 240 kg board is far beyond them, so aids are needed.

questions.q: What is the best way to get the 240 kg board up to the first-floor plant room?
o: Carry it up the stair with six strong people
Tilt it on its side and slide it up the stairs
Use the goods hoist, with the board strapped upright
Take it up in two halves after unbolting the frame
questions.why: Avoid carrying where a lifting aid exists. The hoist, with the load strapped upright and its rating checked above 240 kg, moves the board without anyone bearing its weight. Sliding it on its side or taking it apart can damage it, and a stair carry risks falls.

questions.q: The board is top-heavy and the doorway is 0.8 m wide. What should Rochelle plan for?
o: Pushing it through quickly, so it cannot tip over
Cutting the side panels to make it narrower
Leaving it outside until the doorway is widened
Tilting it with enough people, as the maker allows
questions.why: A load that is too wide upright can often be tilted through, with the maker's agreement, by a planned team. The centre of gravity is high, so it moves slowly and is steadied. Speed makes tipping more likely, and cutting a panel destroys the equipment.

questions.q: Which item belongs in Rochelle's written lift plan for this board?
o: Only the date and the client's name
The cost of the board and of hiring the aids
The weight, route, aids, people, roles and signals
The colour of the cover and the make of the trolley
questions.why: A lift plan is what lets everyone do the move safely and together: the load's weight and centre of gravity, the route, the aids and their ratings, who does what, who leads and spots, and the signals. Costs and colours do not help anyone move the board safely.

questions.q: About how much cable is in the 60 m pull?
o: About 25 kg
About 252 kg
About 4.2 kg
About 2,520 kg
questions.why: Mass = 4.2 kg/m × 60 m = 252 kg. That is a heavy pull for hands alone, so the plan includes the drum on jacks with a brake, rollers, a steady pull and, if the maker allows, a winch.

questions.q: What is the best way to deal with the unchocked drum on the slope?
o: Chock it, and set it up on jacks on level ground
Hold it with a rope tied round a nearby post or tree
Leave it as it is, since it has not rolled so far
Have a trainee stand below it, ready to catch it
questions.why: A drum on a slope can roll away and crush someone. It is chocked at once, and moved to firm level ground, where it is raised on drum jacks with a spindle and a brake. Nobody stands below a drum, and a post is not a reliable restraint.

questions.q: From which part of the drum should the cable leave as it is pulled, and how should the drum be set up?
o: Off the bottom, dragging along the ground behind
Off the side, with a trainee holding the flange still
Off the top, with the drum lying flat on one flange
Off the top, with the drum turning freely on jacks
questions.why: Cable is paid off the top of a drum that is raised on jacks, with a spindle through its centre and a brake, so that it turns freely and does not over-run. Dragging cable from the bottom, or from a drum lying on its flange, kinks and scrapes it.

questions.q: What should Winston say to the trainee about winding the pulling rope round his hand?
o: Yes, if he wears thick leather gloves for the pull
Yes, if he stands at the back of the pulling team
No: a sudden jerk can trap and injure the hand
No: it makes the cable twist inside the duct
questions.why: If the cable suddenly moves or the rope is snatched, a rope wrapped round the hand tightens and can crush or drag the hand. Pullers hold the rope in their gloved hands so that they can let go at once. Gloves do not remove the risk.

questions.q: What is the total mass of the battery bank, and is the stand adequate?
o: 320 kg, so the 300 kg stand is not adequate
320 kg, so the 300 kg stand is adequate
32 kg, so the stand is more than adequate
310 kg, so the 300 kg stand is just adequate
questions.why: 10 × 32 kg = 320 kg, which is more than the stand's 300 kg rating. The stand must be replaced or its rating confirmed before the batteries are placed. The stand and floor must always be checked against the total mass, not against one battery.

questions.q: Which extra precaution should be taken before the batteries are handled?
o: Join the terminals together with a wire so they stay balanced
Fit terminal covers, and remove the ring and watch
Rest a steel bar across the terminals while carrying
Leave the terminals bare so that they can be tested
questions.why: A metal tool, ring or watch strap that bridges the terminals shorts the battery and can cause sparks, burns and an explosion. Insulating covers are fitted and metal jewellery is removed. Joining or bridging terminals deliberately creates that short circuit.

questions.q: How should the 32 kg batteries be moved over the 30 m of gravel?
o: On a small sack truck, pulled over the gravel, strapped
Two at a time, held against the chest by one person
One at a time, dragged along by the carrying handle
On a trolley or carrier, one at a time, over the gravel
questions.why: Gravel is too soft for a small-wheeled sack truck, and 64 kg is far too heavy for one person. A battery carrier or a trolley with large wheels, or two people with the carrying handles, keeps each battery upright. Dragging by the handle can crack the case and spill acid.

questions.q: What should Orlando say about carrying the 48 kg unit up the vertical ladder on a shoulder?
o: Yes, if the ladder is tied at the top and he goes slowly
No: use a hoist or lift aid, as a climber needs both hands
Yes, if he stops to rest halfway up the ladder
No: ask two trainees to carry it up the ladder together
questions.why: A person climbing a ladder must have both hands free, and 48 kg on a shoulder can throw him off. The unit is raised by hoist, gin wheel or lift aid, with a tag line, while people stay clear below. Two people on one ladder is worse.

questions.q: Why should the solar panels not be handled in the gusty afternoon wind?
o: Wind chills the panels, so they are hard to hold
Wind charges the panels with static electricity
A panel can catch the wind like a sail
Wind makes the panels heavier to lift
questions.why: A solar panel is large and light. A gust can lift it, turn it and drag the carriers towards the roof edge, which has no parapet. Panels are moved by two people in calm conditions, laid flat and weighted or tied when set down.

questions.q: What must the team do about the JPS line 4 m from the back of the building?
o: Look up, and keep ladders and long items well clear
Ignore it, since 4 m is far enough away
Cover it with a dry blanket before the work starts
Push it aside with a dry wooden pole to make room
questions.why: Metal ladders, conduit and panel frames that touch or come close to a line can carry deadly current to the holder. Look up before moving or raising anything long, keep well clear as the power company requires, and never touch or move a line. If it is in the way, the supervisor arranges with JPS.

questions.q: What should Carla do first when Shane reports his back pain two days later?
o: Tell him to rest at home, and say nothing more
Ask him to keep working, as it was only a small pain
Give him a lighter job, and keep it to themselves
Make sure he gets first aid and a check, and report it
questions.why: A sharp pain in the back during a lift is an injury that can worsen with work. He should be seen by a first-aider or doctor, and the incident is reported, even though two days late. Reporting finds the cause and protects others.

questions.q: Which finding gets nearest to the cause of Shane's injury?
o: He is careless and should have known better than to lift it
A 45 kg coil was lifted alone, with no aid or assessment
He took a painkiller, and that hid the strain from others
The cable in the coil was too heavy for the job to be done
questions.why: A lone lift of 45 kg from the floor, with no aid, is the hazard that the workshop could have controlled. Looking at the system (no assessment, no trolley, heavy items stored badly) finds fixable causes. Blaming the person does not stop it happening to the next one.

questions.q: Two other staff mention aching backs, and the heavy boxes are on the top shelf. Which change cuts the risk most?
o: Tell staff to lift more carefully from the top shelf
Buy support belts for everyone who works in the store
Move heavy boxes to low shelves, and provide a trolley
Keep the boxes where they are, and have them lifted in pairs
questions.why: Heavy items at waist height need no lifting from above the shoulders, and a trolley removes carrying. Storage and equipment changes come before advice, belts and pairs. Aches that keep coming back are a warning that the job needs to change.

questions.q: Carla suggests a back-support belt for each trainee. What is the right view?
o: It is the best control, as it takes the load off the back
It is useful only for people with a past injury
It should be worn instead of using a trolley
It does not remove the risk and can give false confidence
questions.why: A belt does not strengthen the back or make a load lighter, and wearing one can tempt people to lift more than they should. Avoiding the lift, using aids, reducing the load and improving storage come first.

questions.q: A chain sling's tag shows its last thorough examination was 14 months ago, and the Centre's rule is every 6 months. What should happen?
o: Do not use it until it has been examined again
Use it for light loads only until the next examination
Use it, after looking it over carefully by eye
Use it this once, and book an examination for later
questions.why: The sling is out of date, and nobody knows what damage it may have. It is not used at all, whatever the load, until a competent person has examined it and renewed its tag. A look by eye cannot find hidden wear.

questions.q: A trolley is rated for 220 kg and already carries a 130 kg transformer. Boxes of fittings of 20 kg are to be added. How many may be added?
questions.why: 220 − 130 = 90 kg of capacity remains. 90 ÷ 20 = 4.5, so at most 4 boxes: round down, never up. Remember that the trolley's rating covers everything on it, including straps and tools.
